p: The letter names Paul. Scholars are divided over whether he wrote it or a later follower wrote in his name.
b: The letter says it is from Paul, Silvanus and Timothy, and it closes with a greeting in Paul's own hand (3:17). The church read it as Paul's from the second century on. Since the work of J. E. C. Schmidt (1798) and William Wrede (1903), many scholars have doubted it. Their reasons: it follows 1 Thessalonians very closely, sometimes phrase by phrase, yet sounds cooler and more formal; its teaching that signs must come first (2:3-12) seems to clash with the sudden coming of the thief in 1 Thessalonians 5:2; and its warnings about a letter 'that seems to be from us' (2:2) and its stress on Paul's signature (3:17) can be read as the marks of a writer imitating Paul. Wolfgang Trilling's study and Maarten Menken's commentary argue for a later writer; Abraham Malherbe and Charles Wanamaker defend Paul. A survey at the British New Testament Conference in 2011 found most of the 111 scholars present in favor of Paul, with a large group unsure. The Plain English Translation follows the text and calls the writer Paul. The book page sets out both cases.

p: Paul's partners on the journey that founded the church: Silvanus is the Silas of Acts.
b: Acts calls him Silas; Paul's letters use the name Silvanus (also 2 Corinthians 1:19; 1 Peter 5:12). He was a leader of the Jerusalem church whom Paul chose for his second journey (Acts 15:22, 40), shared his beating and jailing at Philippi (Acts 16:19-40), and helped found the church at Thessalonica: some Jews there "cast in their lot with Paul and Silas" (Acts 17:4). Timothy joined Paul at Lystra (Acts 16:1-3) and stayed behind in Berea: "Silas and Timothy stayed behind in Berea" (Acts 17:14). 1 Thessalonians 3:1-6 says Paul sent him from Athens to Thessalonica and that he came back with good news. Acts later reports: "Once Silas and Timothy had come down from Macedonia" (Acts 18:5), so the three were together in Corinth, which fits a letter sent from there. The same three names open 1 Thessalonians.
r: Acts 15:22; Acts 15:40; Acts 16:19-40; Acts 17:4; Acts 18:5; 2 Corinthians 1:19; 1 Thessalonians 1:1; 1 Peter 5:12; Acts 16:1-3; Acts 17:14; 1 Thessalonians 3:1-6

t: A young church in a capital city
p: Thessalonica was the chief city of the Roman province of Macedonia, on the main road across the Balkans.
b: Thessalonica (modern Thessaloniki in Greece) was a busy port and the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia, on the Via Egnatia, the road that linked Italy with the east. Acts 17:1-9 tells how the church began: Paul spoke in the synagogue for three Sabbaths, some Jews and many God-fearing Greeks and leading women believed, and a crowd dragged Jason and others before the city rulers, shouting that the newcomers said "that Jesus is another king" (Acts 17:7). The believers were mostly Gentiles who had turned away from idols to serve the living God (1 Thessalonians 1:9). They had been believers only months, or a few years, when this letter came.

p: Paul joins a Greek greeting word to the Jewish blessing of peace.
b: Greek letters opened with chairein, "greetings". Paul uses the related word charis, "grace", the free kindness of God, and adds eirene, "peace", the Greek for Hebrew shalom, the old priestly wish that God "grant you peace" (Numbers 6:26). Most of Paul's letters open this way; Colossians has a shorter form, and 1 and 2 Timothy add "mercy". See also the note at 3:16, where the letter closes with peace.
orig: χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη (charis hymin kai eirene)

t: Brothers: a word that includes the sisters
p: The Greek plural adelphoi takes in the whole church, women and men.
b: The Greek plural adelphoi, "brothers", was used for a mixed group, as English once used "men" for everyone; Acts says "many women of the first rank" were among the first believers at Thessalonica (Acts 17:4). The Plain English Translation keeps "brothers", as Romans and Acts do on this site, with a gloss "brothers and sisters". The word appears seven times in this short letter (1:3; 2:1, 13, 15; 3:1, 6, 13), and in 3:6 and 3:15 it reaches even the member who is being disciplined: he is still "a brother".
orig: ἀδελφοί (adelphoi), 'brothers'

p: Paul says thanks is a debt. Some hear duty and coolness; others hear an answer to the readers' modesty.
b: Paul usually writes "I thank God" or "we give thanks". Here and in 2:13 he writes eucharistein opheilomen, "we are bound to give thanks", from the verb for owing a debt. Scholars who doubt that Paul wrote the letter count this as part of its more formal, cooler tone, set beside the warmth of 1 Thessalonians 1-3. Another reading: Paul is saying he cannot help praising them, perhaps because they had protested that they did not deserve the praise of his first letter; "it is only right" makes the same point. Both readings fit the Greek.
orig: εὐχαριστεῖν ὀφείλομεν (eucharistein opheilomen), 'we are obligated to give thanks'

p: The letter does not describe the pressure; Acts and 1 Thessalonians give a picture of it.
b: Two words: diogmoi, "persecutions", pursuit by opponents, and thlipseis, "troubles", pressure of every kind (this site's word for thlipsis). Acts shows a mob and a court at the very start (Acts 17:5-9), and 1 Thessalonians 2:14 says the believers suffered at the hands of their own countrymen, that is, Gentile neighbors. For converts who had left the gods of their city and family, the pressure may have been social and economic as much as legal: lost trade, family anger, suspicion of disloyalty to the emperor's cult. The letter speaks of it as still going on ("you are bearing").
orig: διωγμοῖς ... θλίψεσιν (diogmois ... thlipsesin)

a: a plain sign of God's just judgment
p: The Greek does not say what the sign is: the readers' suffering, or the faith and endurance they show in it.
b: The word endeigma, "evidence, proof", stands without a verb. Most readers take it to point back to the whole of 1:4: that the believers keep their faith under persecution shows that God is at work and that his verdict at the end will be just, putting them in the right and their persecutors in the wrong. Philippians 1:28 makes a similar point with a related word. Others take the sign to be the suffering itself, as God's way of making his people fit for his kingdom (compare Acts 14:22). The Plain English Translation keeps the open wording of the Greek. The verb behind "counted worthy", kataxioo, means to count or declare someone worthy: a verdict, not a payment, and the prayer of 1:11 asks God to give it. The point is not that pain buys a place in the kingdom, but that those who suffer for it will be judged to belong to it (compare Luke 20:35 and Acts 5:41, the same verb family).
orig: ἔνδειγμα τῆς δικαίας κρίσεως τοῦ θεοῦ (endeigma tes dikaias kriseos tou theou)

p: The letter leaves vengeance to God, as the Torah and Paul elsewhere do.
b: The verb antapodidomi, "to give back", is the word of just payment. The thought is the Song of Moses: "Vengeance belongs to me, and payback" (Deuteronomy 32:35), quoted in Romans 12:19 to tell believers not to take revenge themselves. The Greek of Isaiah 66:15 also has God "paying back" his enemies with fire, and 1:8 goes on to borrow that picture. The readers are not told to strike back; 1 Thessalonians 5:15 forbids it. They are told that God is not blind to what is being done to them. In return the troubled are given "rest" (1:7, anesis), a loosening or relaxation, the word Paul sets against thlipsis, "pressure, trouble" (2 Corinthians 7:5; 2 Corinthians 8:13): those who press hard will be pressed, and those who are pressed will be eased. Paul includes himself ("and to us with you").
r: Deuteronomy 32:35; Romans 12:19; Isaiah 66:15; 1 Thessalonians 5:15; 2 Corinthians 7:5; 2 Corinthians 8:13

a: the revealing of the Lord Jesus from heaven
p: The coming of Christ is called an unveiling: what is hidden now will be seen.
b: The noun is apokalypsis, "uncovering, revealing", the word behind "apocalypse". Paul uses it for Christ's coming also in 1 Corinthians 1:7: "as you eagerly wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Corinthians 1:7). The letter speaks of three ways the end arrives: Christ's "revealing" (here), his "coming" (parousia, 2:1, 8) and his "appearing" (epiphaneia, 2:8). Chapter 2 then uses the verb of the same word for the lawless one, who must "be revealed" (2:3, 6, 8): a false unveiling that comes before the true one.
orig: ἐν τῇ ἀποκαλύψει τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ (en te apokalypsei tou kyriou Iesou)

t: The Lord comes with his angels
p: Old Testament pictures of God's coming are applied to Jesus.
b: In Zechariah, God comes to fight for Jerusalem: "And the LORD my God will arrive, and all the holy ones will be with you" (Zechariah 14:5). In Daniel's vision the judge sits surrounded by countless attendants (Daniel 7:10). Jesus uses the same picture of the Son of Man: "When the Son of Man comes in his glory and all the angels come with him" (Matthew 25:31). Here the angels belong to "the Lord Jesus": the role of Israel's God in the old texts is given to him. "Angels of his power" may be a Hebrew-style phrase for "his mighty angels", or angels who carry out his power.
orig: μετ' ἀγγέλων δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ (met' angelon dynameos autou)

p: The phrase is the Greek of Isaiah 66:15, where the LORD comes in fire to judge.
b: The Greek Old Testament of Isaiah 66:15 ends "in a flame of fire" (en phlogi pyros), and the verse also has God "paying back" and bringing ekdikesis, "punishment", the two words of 1:6 and 1:8. The site's Plain English Translation of Isaiah 66:15, from the Hebrew, reads: "For look, the LORD will come in fire, / and his chariots like the storm wind" (Isaiah 66:15). Fire also marks God's appearing at the burning bush (Exodus 3:2) and Sinai (Exodus 19:18). Here it is "the Lord Jesus" who comes in that fire. The editions differ on the word order here ("a flame of fire" or "a fire of flame"; see the variant); the meaning is the same.
orig: ἐν φλογὶ πυρός (en phlogi pyros); some editions πυρὶ φλογός

a: people who do not know God
p: Those who 'do not know God' and those who 'will not obey the good news' may be the same people or two groups.
b: The Greek repeats the article: "to those who do not know God, and to those who do not obey the good news". The first phrase echoes Jeremiah's prayer: "Pour out your fury on the nations that have not known you" (Jeremiah 10:25), which in the Bible usually means Gentiles. So some read two groups: Gentiles who never knew God, and Jews who heard the message and refused it. Others read one group described twice, in the style of Hebrew poetry: the persecutors of the Thessalonian church, who were themselves mostly Gentiles (1 Thessalonians 2:14). On that reading the letter speaks of those who were attacking the readers, not of every unbeliever in history.

t: Eternal ruin: what does it mean?
p: Readers have taken it as endless punishment, as a final end, or as a ruin from which God still rescues.
b: The phrase olethron aionion occurs only here in the New Testament. Olethros is ruin or destruction; the Plain English Translation says "ruin", as it does for the same word in 1 Corinthians 5:5 and 1 Thessalonians 5:3. It is not the word behind "the son of ruin" in 2:3 and "on the road to ruin" in 2:10 (apoleia, apollymi): English has one word where the Greek has two. Aionios is "of the age (to come)", usually "eternal". Three main readings: (1) eternal conscious punishment: a ruin that never ends, separation from God's presence forever, the traditional teaching of most churches; (2) final destruction (often called conditional immortality or annihilationism): the result is permanent, but the lost cease to exist; held by Seventh-day Adventists and by a minority of evangelicals, among them Edward Fudge; (3) a hope of final restoration: "of the age" names the quality or the time of the penalty, not its endlessness; a minority reading. The card on the chapter page sets out what the churches teach.
orig: ὄλεθρον αἰώνιον (olethron aionion)

a: from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his strength
p: The phrase is the Greek of Isaiah 2:10, 19 and 21, where people hide from the LORD's terror.
b: The Greek Old Testament of Isaiah 2:10 has, word for word, "from the face of ... the Lord and from the glory of his strength", and repeats it in 2:19 and 2:21. The site's Plain English Translation of the Hebrew reads: "away from the dread of the LORD / and his majestic splendor" (Isaiah 2:10). In Isaiah, the proud crawl into caves on the day the LORD rises. The Greek preposition apo, "from", can mean "away from" (cut off from the Lord's presence) or "coming from" (the destruction comes from his face and glory, as fire comes from him in 1:8). Isaiah's picture, people fleeing away from his presence, supports the first; the fire of 1:8 supports the second. The Plain English Translation keeps "from" so that both stay open.
orig: ἀπὸ προσώπου τοῦ κυρίου καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς δόξης τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ (apo prosopou tou kyriou kai apo tes doxes tes ischyos autou)

t: His saints: angels, believers, or both?
p: 'Holy ones' can mean angels or God's people; the Psalms' Greek has God glorified among them.
b: Hagioi, "holy ones", is this site's "the saints" (God's holy people). In Zechariah 14:5 the holy ones who come with the LORD are angels, and 1:7 has just spoken of angels. But the parallel line, "everyone who has believed", suggests people. The words echo the Greek of Psalm 89:7 (88:8 in the Greek numbering), "God, glorified in the council of the holy ones"; the site's Plain English Translation of the Hebrew reads: "a God dreaded in the inner council of the holy ones" (Psalm 89:7). Most readers take the saints here to be believers, in whom Christ's glory will be seen. Glory "in" them may mean glory shown in their changed lives, or glory given among them, as a king is honored in his court.
orig: ἐνδοξασθῆναι ἐν τοῖς ἁγίοις αὐτοῦ (endoxasthenai en tois hagiois autou)

p: The prophets' 'that day' of the LORD becomes the day of the Lord Jesus.
b: In the Greek the words "on that day" stand at the very end of the sentence, with weight. "That day" is the prophets' phrase for the day of the LORD (Isaiah 2:11, 17, 20; Zechariah 14:4-9). The next chapter turns on exactly this question: has that day already come (2:2)? See the topic page on the day of the Lord.
orig: ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ (en te hemera ekeine)

a: every good thing you long to do
p: The Greek says 'every good pleasure of goodness': God's good purpose, or the readers' desire to do good.
b: Eudokia often means God's good pleasure (Ephesians 1:5, 9; Philippians 2:13), and some read the phrase as "every good purpose of God". But it is paired with "every work of faith", which is surely the readers' own, and agathosyne, "goodness", is a human quality in Paul (Galatians 5:22; Romans 15:14). So most translations, and the Plain English Translation, take it as the readers' desire for good, which God will bring to completion.
orig: εὐδοκίαν ἀγαθωσύνης (eudokian agathosynes)

a: the name of our Lord Jesus will have glory in you
p: Christ's name honored in them, and they honored in him: Isaiah's words about the servant and God's name.
b: The Greek of Isaiah 66:5 has "so that the name of the Lord may be glorified", where the Hebrew, in the site's Plain English Translation, has the scoffers say "'Let the LORD show his glory'" (Isaiah 66:5); 1:8 has already borrowed from Isaiah 66. God also says of his servant Israel: "through you I will win glory" (Isaiah 49:3). The new step is that the divine name to be honored is "our Lord Jesus", and that the glory runs both ways: he in them, and they in him.

a: our God and the Lord Jesus Christ
t: Two persons, or 'our God and Lord, Jesus Christ'?
p: The Greek has one article; some read the phrase as calling Jesus God. The Plain English Translation keeps two persons.
b: The Greek is tou theou hemon kai kyriou Iesou Christou. When two nouns share one article, they often name the same person, and on that basis some read "of our God and Lord, Jesus Christ", as in Titus 2:13 and 2 Peter 1:1, where many translations do read it so. The Plain English Translation keeps two persons here, as the KJV does, because "Lord Jesus Christ" works like a proper name, which the rule does not cover, and because Paul often pairs "God our Father" and "the Lord Jesus Christ" (1:1, 2). 2:16 has its own surprise: the Lord Jesus Christ named before God the Father.
orig: τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν καὶ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (tou theou hemon kai kyriou Iesou Christou)

p: The word for a ruler's arrival in a city. The lawless one has his own 'coming' too (2:9).
b: Parousia means "presence" or "arrival". In later Greek it was the usual word for the visit of a king, as Abbott-Smith's lexicon notes. Paul uses it for Christ's return (1 Thessalonians 2:19; 3:13; 4:15; 5:23; 1 Corinthians 15:23), and Matthew 24:3, 27 uses it in Jesus' own words. This chapter uses it three times: Christ's coming (2:1, 8) and, in a dark parody, the lawless one's coming (2:9).
orig: παρουσία (parousia), 'arrival, presence'

p: The word for the great ingathering at the end, which the Gospels give to the Son of Man's angels.
b: The noun episynagoge occurs only here and in Hebrews 10:25. The verb is the Gospels' word for the end: the Son of Man "will send out the angels and gather together his chosen from the four winds" (Mark 13:27; compare Matthew 24:31). The hope goes back to Israel's prophets, who promised that God would gather his scattered people (Deuteronomy 30:4; Isaiah 11:12). The readers knew the picture from 1 Thessalonians 4:17, where those still alive are caught up to meet the Lord. Whether that meeting is a separate "rapture" before the troubles of 2:3-12 is debated; see the topic page and the card on the chapter page. The verse opens with hyper, "concerning, on the subject of"; the KJV's "by the coming" can sound like an oath, which the Greek does not mean here.
orig: ἡμῶν ἐπισυναγωγῆς ἐπ' αὐτόν (hemon episynagoges ep' auton)
r: Mark 13:27; Matthew 24:31; Hebrews 10:25; Deuteronomy 30:4; Isaiah 11:12; 1 Thessalonians 4:17

a: a letter that seems to be from us
t: A forged letter, or a misread one?
p: Someone was claiming Paul's authority for the idea that the day had come. How, the letter does not say.
b: Three channels are named: "a spirit" (a prophecy spoken in the church, compare 1 Thessalonians 5:19-21), "a word" (a teaching or a report), and "a letter". "As if from us" may go with the letter only, or with all three. The readers may have received a forged letter in Paul's name; or someone may have misread 1 Thessalonians, which had said the day comes the way a thief comes at night (1 Thessalonians 5:2). Those who think a later writer composed 2 Thessalonians find an irony here: the letter that warns against a false letter from Paul may itself be one, written to correct how 1 Thessalonians was being read. Those who hold that Paul wrote it say that he knew false claims were made in his name and answers with his signature (3:17). The Westminster Confession lists this verse among its proofs that nothing may be added to Scripture "by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men" (1.6).

p: The KJV's 'at hand' sounds like 'coming soon'. The Greek perfect means it has arrived.
b: Enesteken is the perfect of enistemi, "to be present, to have come". Paul uses it for "things present" against "things to come" (Romans 8:38; 1 Corinthians 3:22). The KJV's "the day of Christ is at hand" can make a modern reader think the problem was people saying the end was near, which Paul himself taught. The claim was stronger: the day had already begun. How anyone could think so is unclear. They may have thought the end-time troubles they were suffering were the day itself, or held a spiritual view that the resurrection had already happened (compare 2 Timothy 2:18), or taken a prophecy literally.
orig: ἐνέστηκεν (enesteken), 'has come, is present'

p: A revolt against God. A minority reading takes it as 'the departure', the rapture.
b: Apostasia means "defection, revolt". In the Greek Old Testament it is rebellion against God: "If this was rebellion" (Joshua 22:22), where the Greek has this word; 1 Maccabees 2:15 uses it of Antiochus' forced paganism: "The king's officers who were enforcing the apostasy" (1 Maccabees 2:15). Its only other New Testament use is the charge that Paul taught Jews "to desert Moses" (Acts 21:21). With the article, "the rebellion" is one the readers already knew about (2:5): a great falling away or revolt at the end (compare Matthew 24:10-12). Whether it is a revolt within the church, of the world against God, or both, is debated. Some pre-tribulation teachers, such as Thomas Ice, argue that the word here means a physical "departure", the rapture of the church before the man of lawlessness appears. Most translations and interpreters keep "rebellion" or "apostasy", because that is how the word is used elsewhere.
orig: ἡ ἀποστασία (he apostasia)

p: A Hebrew-style phrase: a man whose nature is lawlessness, the opposite of God's rule.
b: "Man of lawlessness" is a Semitic way of saying "the utterly lawless man". Anomia, "lawlessness", is more than breaking rules: it is defiance of God's order, the word of Jesus' warning: "Lawlessness will multiply, and because of it the love of many will go cold" (Matthew 24:12). The chapter repeats it: "the mystery of lawlessness" (2:7) and "the lawless one" (2:8). The Byzantine text and the KJV read "the man of sin" (see the variant). Christians later joined this figure to Daniel's "little horn", Revelation's beast and John's word "antichrist" (1 John 2:18), but Paul does not use that word.
orig: ὁ ἄνθρωπος τῆς ἀνομίας (ho anthropos tes anomias)

p: The same Greek phrase that John uses for Judas.
b: "Son of ruin" is a Hebrew idiom: one who belongs to ruin and is headed for it. The Greek is the same as in Jesus' prayer about Judas: "none of them was ruined except the son of ruin" (John 17:12). The Greek of Isaiah 57:4 calls the faithless of Israel "children of ruin, a lawless seed", putting the two words of this verse side by side. Apoleia, "ruin", is the fate of those "on the road to ruin" in 2:10, a word from the same root. The KJV's "son of perdition" is the same phrase.
orig: ὁ υἱὸς τῆς ἀπωλείας (ho huios tes apoleias)

a: lifts himself up over everything people call a god or worship
p: The picture comes from Daniel 11, where the king who exalts himself is first Antiochus IV.
b: Daniel's last vision describes a king who defiles the sanctuary: "Above every god he will raise himself, and he will make himself great" (Daniel 11:36), and "because he will lift himself above everything" (Daniel 11:37). The Greek of Theodotion's Daniel 11:36 is close to Paul's words: the king "will be exalted and made great over every god" (epi panta theon), with different verbs from Paul's. The first reference of Daniel's vision is Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who in 167 BC set up "the abomination that desolates" in the Temple (Daniel 11:31; 1 Maccabees 1:54). Jesus took up Daniel's words for a future desecration (Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14). The word sebasma, "object of worship", is the one Paul used in Athens for the city's shrines (Acts 17:23).
r: Daniel 11:36-37; Daniel 11:31; Daniel 7:25; Daniel 8:11; 1 Maccabees 1:54; Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14; Acts 17:23

p: Naos is the inner house where the god lives, not the whole temple area.
b: Paul's word is naos, the shrine or inner house of a god, not hieron, the temple complex with its courts. The Gospels and Acts on this site call the naos "the sanctuary"; in Paul's letters it is "temple" (1 Corinthians 3:16-17; 6:19; 2 Corinthians 6:16), where Paul uses it for the believers as the place God lives. Which temple is meant here is the question of the next note.
orig: ναός (naos), 'shrine, inner house'

p: The Jerusalem Temple, a temple rebuilt in the future, the church, or a picture of claiming God's place.
b: (1) The Jerusalem Temple, still standing when the letter was written. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.25) took it so, of a final Antichrist. The readers would remember Gaius Caligula's order in AD 40 to set up his statue "in the temple of God" (Josephus, Antiquities 18.261; also Philo's Embassy to Gaius), an order never carried out. Rodger Young and Andrew Steinmann, in a study of its date, think the episode would probably have been in Paul's mind. (2) A temple rebuilt in the future in Jerusalem, the dispensational reading, linked to Daniel 9:27. (3) The church, which Paul elsewhere calls God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16): Augustine noted that some took it so (City of God 20.19), and the Reformers applied it to the papacy (see the card). (4) A picture: the man claims God's own seat, as the ruler of Tyre said: "I am a god! I sit in a seat for gods" (Ezekiel 28:2). Augustine himself said it is "uncertain in what temple he shall sit". For dating, those who read (1) note that the letter seems to assume the Temple stands, which fits a date before AD 70; those who date the letter later answer that a writer after AD 70 could take the picture from Daniel without a standing temple in view.
r: Ezekiel 28:2; Daniel 9:27; Daniel 11:31; 1 Corinthians 3:16; Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14

p: Rulers who claimed to be gods: the king of Tyre, Antiochus 'Epiphanes', and the emperors.
b: Ezekiel mocks the ruler of Tyre: "But you are a human being and not a god, though you make your heart like the heart of a god" (Ezekiel 28:2). Antiochus IV took the title Epiphanes, "(God) Made Manifest" (1 Maccabees 1:10). Roman emperors were honored as gods in the cities of the East, and Gaius demanded worship as a god in his lifetime. Greek readers knew what such a claim looked like.
orig: ἀποδεικνύντα ἑαυτὸν ὅτι ἔστιν θεός (apodeiknynta heauton hoti estin theos)

p: In a short stay, Paul taught the new believers about the end in detail. The letter assumes they remember.
b: The tense is "I was saying", repeated teaching. Acts says Paul spoke in the synagogue "for three Sabbaths" (Acts 17:2), though the believers' gifts sent to him at Philippi (Philippians 4:16) suggest he stayed longer. In that time he taught Gentile converts the Jewish hope of the end: the day of the Lord, the resurrection, the final enemy. The singular "I" breaks into the letter's "we", as in 1 Thessalonians 2:18; 3:5. Because the readers knew what he had said, Paul can write in hints ("you know", 2:6), and later readers cannot fill in all the gaps.

t: What, and who, is holding him back?
p: The neuter 'what' (2:6) becomes 'the one' (2:7). The readers knew; we do not, and Augustine said so.
b: Paul writes to katechon, "the thing that holds back" (neuter), and in 2:7 ho katechon, "the one who holds back" (masculine). The readings: (1) the Roman Empire and its emperor, law and order holding back chaos: Tertullian ("What obstacle is there but the Roman state", On the Resurrection of the Flesh 24) and John Chrysostom, who knew some said "the grace of the Spirit" but sided with "the Roman empire" (Homily 4 on 2 Thessalonians); (2) the Holy Spirit, working through the church, removed at the rapture: the pre-tribulation dispensational reading (Thomas Ice); (3) God himself, or his set plan, holding the end until its time; (4) the preaching of the gospel to the nations (Mark 13:10), with Paul as the one preaching it; (5) the archangel Michael, "the great prince who stands guard over the sons of your people" (Daniel 12:1); (6) an evil power, since katecho can mean "seize, occupy": the one who now holds sway. Augustine, after surveying the views, wrote: "I frankly confess I do not know what he means" (City of God 20.19). "Now" may go with "you know" or with "holding back".
orig: τὸ κατέχον ... ὁ κατέχων (to katechon ... ho katechon)

p: The evil that will be revealed is already active, hidden, in the present.
b: Mysterion in Paul is a secret of God now made known (Romans 11:25; 16:25). Here, set against that, is a dark secret: lawlessness already working beneath the surface, before its person is revealed. John says much the same when he speaks of many antichrists already in the world (1 John 2:18). Chrysostom thought Paul meant Nero, "as if he were the type of Antichrist" (Homily 4), and Augustine reports that some took it so. The point for the readers is that evil now, including their persecution, is real but limited: the full revealing is held back.
orig: τὸ μυστήριον ... τῆς ἀνομίας (to mysterion ... tes anomias)

a: until he is gone from the scene
p: A Greek idiom: 'until he comes out of the middle', that is, until he is removed or steps aside.
b: Heos ek mesou genetai, literally "until he becomes out of the middle", is a common way of saying "until he is removed". It does not say who removes him, or whether he steps aside. The KJV's "until he be taken out of the way" made the passive reading familiar; the Plain English Translation keeps the open sense. Readers who take the restrainer as the Holy Spirit present in the church see here the church's removal at the rapture (Thomas Ice); readers who take it as Rome see the fall of the empire (Tertullian). The grammar also allows the lawless one himself to be the subject, coming "out of the midst"; the Plain English Translation reads it of the one holding him back, the subject of the same sentence.
orig: ἕως ἐκ μέσου γένηται (heos ek mesou genetai)

t: Isaiah's king who kills with his breath
p: The Messiah of Isaiah 11 defeats the wicked with a word. Paul's verb is the Greek of Isaiah 11:4.
b: Isaiah's shoot of Jesse needs no army: "His mouth will be a rod to strike the earth, / and the breath of his lips will put the wicked to death" (Isaiah 11:4). The Greek of Isaiah has the same verb, anelei, "he will do away with", and the same word pneuma, "breath, spirit". Revelation draws on the same text: "From his mouth comes a sharp sword to strike the nations with" (Revelation 19:15). The lawless one, with all his signs (2:9), falls to a breath.
orig: τῷ πνεύματι τοῦ στόματος αὐτοῦ (to pneumati tou stomatos autou)

p: Two words for the arrival of a god or king, stacked together.
b: Epiphaneia, "appearing", was used for a god showing himself, and for the arrival of a ruler; Antiochus IV called himself Epiphanes. Parousia, "coming", is the royal visit (see 2:1). Paul puts them together, "the appearing of his coming": the coming will be seen, and its brightness alone undoes the lawless one. Elsewhere in the New Testament epiphaneia is the word of the letters to Timothy and Titus (1 Timothy 6:14; 2 Timothy 1:10; 2 Timothy 4:1, 8; Titus 2:13); outside those letters, this is its only use in Paul. Both the Pastoral letters and 2 Thessalonians are among the letters whose authorship is disputed (see the book page).
orig: τῇ ἐπιφανείᾳ τῆς παρουσίας αὐτοῦ (te epiphaneia tes parousias autou)

p: The lawless one has his own 'coming', 'revealing', signs and wonders: a mirror image of Christ.
b: The same word, parousia, is used of Christ (2:8) and of the lawless one (2:9). He too is "revealed" (2:3, 6, 8), works "signs and wonders", the phrase used for Moses' and Jesus' miracles (Acts 2:22; 7:36), and calls for faith (2:11-12). The picture is the one Jesus gave: "They will give great signs and wonders, so that even the chosen would be led astray, if that were possible" (Matthew 24:24). Revelation's second beast does the same: "It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to the earth in front of people" (Revelation 13:13). His power is real but borrowed: it is "Satan's working".

p: Those 'perishing' share the fate of the 'son of ruin' (2:3): the Greek words are related.
b: Apollymenoi, "those who are perishing", is the present participle of the verb behind apoleia, "ruin" (2:3). The present tense means a course already under way, not yet complete, as in 1 Corinthians 1:18: "For those who are perishing, the word of the cross is foolishness" (1 Corinthians 1:18). What sets them on that road is stated plainly: they "did not accept the love of the truth". It is not that they never heard the truth, but that they would not love it.
orig: τοῖς ἀπολλυμένοις (tois apollymenois)

a: a working that leads them astray
p: God gives people over to the lie they chose. Readers differ on how to hold this with God's goodness.
b: The word is energeia, "working", the same word as "Satan's working" in 2:9; the Plain English Translation says "working" both times so that the link shows: what Satan does, God also, in another sense, sends. The pattern is old: God lets a lying spirit lure Ahab (1 Kings 22:19-23), and in Romans those who reject the truth are handed over: "God handed them over to impurity" (Romans 1:24). The order matters: first they refused the love of the truth (2:10), then God confirms their choice, and the outcome is judgment (2:12, krithosin, "they may be judged", here plainly against them) on two faults set side by side: they "refused to believe the truth" and "took pleasure in unrighteousness". Some readers stress God's active and just judgment; others stress that God permits rather than causes, and that the human refusal came first. The KJV's "strong delusion" made the phrase famous.
orig: πέμπει αὐτοῖς ὁ θεὸς ἐνέργειαν πλάνης (pempei autois ho theos energeian planes)
r: 1 Kings 22:19-23; Romans 1:24; Romans 1:28; Isaiah 6:9-10; Ezekiel 14:9; 2:9-10; Romans 1:18; Romans 2:8; John 3:18-19; 1 Corinthians 13:6

p: With the article: one particular lie, the man's claim to be God (2:4).
b: Greek to pseudos has the article, "the lie". The nearest lie in the chapter is the lawless one's claim that he is God (2:4), backed by "signs and wonders that are a lie" (2:9). Romans uses the same phrase of humanity's first idolatry: "They swapped the truth of God for the lie" (Romans 1:25). In both places the lie is putting a creature in God's place.
orig: τῷ ψεύδει (to pseudei), 'the lie'

p: The phrase is the Greek of Moses' blessing on Benjamin, Paul's own tribe, made plural.
b: This is my own suggestion, not a view found in the sources checked for this book. The Greek egapemenoi hypo kyriou, "loved by the Lord", is the phrase of the Greek Deuteronomy 33:12, the blessing on Benjamin, in the plural (Deuteronomy has the singular, egapemenos hypo kyriou); the site's Plain English Translation of the Hebrew reads: "The LORD's beloved will live in safety by him" (Deuteronomy 33:12). Paul calls himself "of the tribe of Benjamin" (Romans 11:1). If the echo is meant, Paul gives his Gentile converts the blessing of his own tribe: the "beloved of the Lord" who dwell in safety, set against the persecution they suffer. 1 Thessalonians 1:4 has a similar phrase, loved by God, without the echo. The link may be accidental; the phrase is natural Greek.

p: A rare verb for choosing, the one Deuteronomy's Greek uses for God taking Israel as his own people.
b: Paul usually says eklegomai ("choose", Ephesians 1:4). Here he uses haireomai, found in the Greek of Deuteronomy 26:18 in exactly this form, heilato, of the LORD choosing Israel to be "his own private treasure" (Deuteronomy 26:18). What was said of Israel is said of Gentile believers in Thessalonica. How God's choice relates to human faith (here "by faith in the truth") is a lasting question between the churches: see the election topic and the card at Ephesians 1.
orig: εἵλατο ὑμᾶς ὁ θεός (heilato hymas ho theos)

p: The first part of the harvest, given to God as a pledge of the rest.
b: If this reading is right (see the variant), the Thessalonians are "firstfruits": the first sheaf given to God before the harvest is gathered (Leviticus 23:10). Paul uses the word for the first converts in a region: "Epaenetus ... the firstfruits of Asia for Christ" (Romans 16:5; 1 Corinthians 16:15), for Christ raised "the firstfruits" (1 Corinthians 15:23), and for the Spirit (Romans 8:23). The Thessalonians were not the first church in Macedonia: Philippi came before them (Acts 16-17; 1 Thessalonians 2:2). So if this reading is right, the word more likely means that they are the first of a harvest God is still gathering, a pledge of many more.
orig: ἀπαρχήν (aparchen), 'firstfruit'
r: Leviticus 23:10; Romans 16:5; 1 Corinthians 16:15; 1 Corinthians 15:23; Romans 8:23; James 1:18; Acts 16:12-40; 1 Thessalonians 2:2

a: by the Spirit who makes you holy
p: 'In holiness of spirit': the Holy Spirit's work, or the readers' own spirit made holy.
b: The Greek is en hagiasmo pneumatos, "in sanctification of spirit". It can name the Holy Spirit as the one who makes holy, so that 2:13-14 names God, the Lord and the Spirit together, as 1 Peter 1:2 does; or it can mean the readers' own spirit made holy. The Plain English Translation takes the first. "Sanctification" (hagiasmos) is the theme of 1 Thessalonians 4:3-7, where it means a holy life, sexual faithfulness above all.
orig: ἐν ἁγιασμῷ πνεύματος (en hagiasmo pneumatos)

p: What is handed on: Paul's teaching passed down by speech and by letter. A key verse in the debate over tradition.
b: Paradosis is "what is handed over", the word for a teaching passed from teacher to pupil, used of the Pharisees' tradition (Mark 7:8) and of the gospel Paul received and passed on (1 Corinthians 11:2, 23; 15:3). Here it is apostolic teaching, "whether we taught them by speaking or in our letter". The Catholic Church cites this verse for Tradition handed on beside Scripture (Second Vatican Council, Dei Verbum 8); Protestant churches answer that what Paul taught by speech is the same gospel now written down, and that only what is written can now be checked. The card on the chapter page sets out the churches' teaching. In 3:6 the same word refers back to Paul's teaching on work.
orig: τὰς παραδόσεις (tas paradoseis)

p: Most naturally 1 Thessalonians; on Wanamaker's order of the two letters, an earlier letter now lost.
b: The aorist "you were taught ... by our letter" points to an earlier letter, most naturally 1 Thessalonians. That fits Paul writing soon after it. Scholars who think a later writer composed 2 Thessalonians read the verse as a claim to stand in line with the genuine first letter (or, in some views, to correct the way it was being read; compare 2:2). On Charles Wanamaker's view that this letter was written first, carried by Timothy (1 Thessalonians 3:1-5), the letter meant here cannot be 1 Thessalonians, and must be one that has not survived.

a: Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father
t: Christ named first; one verb for both
p: Jesus is named before the Father, and the verbs that follow are singular.
b: Paul usually names God the Father first (1 Thessalonians 3:11); here, as in 2 Corinthians 13:14, the Lord Jesus Christ comes first. The verbs that follow are singular: "who loved" and "gave" (2:16), "may he comfort" and "make strong" (2:17). The Plain English Translation keeps the singular ("he gave", "May he"). Some read here an early sign of what the church later taught as the oneness of the Father and the Son; others note that a singular verb after two subjects is ordinary Greek, agreeing with the nearer subject. Either way, the prayer is addressed to both.
orig: αὐτὸς δὲ ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς καὶ θεὸς ὁ πατὴρ ἡμῶν ... παρακαλέσαι ... στηρίξαι

p: Psalm 147 says God's word runs; Paul asks that the Lord's message race on, and that he be rescued from opponents.
b: The verb is trecho, "run". The Greek of Psalm 147 (verse 4 in the Greek numbering) says "his word will run swiftly"; the site's Plain English Translation of the Hebrew reads: "his word comes running, fast" (Psalm 147:15). Paul, a lover of racing images (1 Corinthians 9:24-26; Philippians 3:14), pictures the message as a runner, and wants for the place he is writing from what happened at Thessalonica (1 Thessalonians 1:8). He also asks to be rescued from "people who are twisted and evil" (3:2; atopos, "out of place", improper, perverse). If Paul wrote from Corinth, this fits Acts 18: Jews there opposed and insulted him (Acts 18:6) and later brought him before the proconsul Gallio (Acts 18:12-17). Paul names no one. Those who date the letter later read the verse as part of a general portrait of Paul the persecuted apostle.
orig: ἵνα ὁ λόγος τοῦ κυρίου τρέχῃ (hina ho logos tou kyriou treche)
r: Psalm 147:15; 1 Thessalonians 1:8; 1 Corinthians 9:24-26; Acts 13:48-49; Acts 18:6; Acts 18:12-17; Romans 15:31; 2 Timothy 3:11

t: The faithful Lord, and the evil one
p: Not everyone has faith, but the Lord is faithful. And "the evil one" can also be read "evil".
b: 3:2 ends ou gar panton he pistis, "for not of all is the faith" (the faith as belief, or faith as trust); 3:3 answers on the same root: pistos de estin ho kyrios, "but faithful is the Lord". Human faith fails in many; the Lord's faithfulness does not (compare 1 Thessalonians 5:24; 1 Corinthians 1:9). Tou ponerou may be "the evil one" or "evil" in general. The same phrase ends the Lord's Prayer in Matthew, which the site renders "rescue us from the evil one" (Matthew 6:13), and Jesus prays: "I am asking you to keep them safe from the evil one" (John 17:15). After a chapter about Satan's working (2:9), the personal reading fits well, and the Plain English Translation follows it, as in Matthew and John on this site.
orig: ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ (apo tou ponerou)
r: Matthew 6:13; John 17:15; 2:9; Ephesians 6:16; 1 John 5:18-19; 3:3; 1 Thessalonians 5:24; 1 Corinthians 1:9; 2 Timothy 2:13

t: Christ's endurance, or waiting for Christ?
p: The KJV reads 'the patient waiting for Christ'. The Greek is 'the endurance of Christ'.
b: Hypomone is endurance, staying power under pressure (this site's word; see 1:4). "The endurance of Christ" may mean the endurance Christ showed in his suffering, which the readers are to share; that reading rests on the word's usual sense in the New Testament and on the pairing with "the love of God" (God's love for them, or their love for God). The KJV's "patient waiting for Christ" takes it as waiting for his return, which fits the letter's theme, and the Greek allows it: in the Greek Old Testament hypomone also means hope or expectation with the Lord as its object (Psalm 39:7; Psalm 71:5; Jeremiah 14:8; Jeremiah 17:13, each in the Greek), where the Hebrew has the word for hope.
orig: εἰς τὴν ὑπομονὴν τοῦ Χριστοῦ (eis ten hypomonen tou Christou)
r: 1:4; Hebrews 12:1-3; Revelation 1:9; Romans 5:5; Psalm 39:7; Psalm 71:5; Jeremiah 14:8

p: A military word, 'out of rank'. Idle, or unruly? The Plain English Translation keeps a phrase that allows both.
b: Ataktos means out of order, out of place, and was used often of soldiers not keeping the ranks (Abbott-Smith's lexicon); so anyone who does not keep to order. In this chapter the disorder shows itself as refusing to work (3:8-12), so many translations say "idle" (the KJV has "disorderly"). The question is whether the word itself means "idle" or whether idleness is the form the disorder took. 1 Thessalonians 5:14 already told the church to warn the ataktoi. The Plain English Translation uses "out of line" in 3:6, 7 and 11, so that the reader can see the same word each time. In 3:11 the Greek plays on one root: meden ergazomenous alla periergazomenous, "doing no work but doing busywork"; the Plain English Translation imitates it with "doing no work at all but working hard at". The cure in 3:12 is to work "quietly" (meta hesychias), the settled life 1 Thessalonians 4:11-12 had already urged.
orig: ἀτάκτως περιπατοῦντος (ataktos peripatountos)
r: 1 Thessalonians 5:14; 3:7; 3:11; 1 Thessalonians 4:11-12; 1 Timothy 5:13; Acts 19:19; 1 Thessalonians 4:11; 1 Timothy 2:2; 3:10

t: Keeping apart: what kind of discipline?
p: The church is to keep its distance from the idle member; the letter limits it: 3:15 says he remains a brother.
b: The verb stellesthai means "to keep one's distance, avoid". 3:14 adds "do not mix with him", the same verb as 1 Corinthians 5:9, 11. The aim is shame that leads to change (3:14), and the limit is set at once: "do not treat him like an enemy" (3:15). Interpreters differ on whether this meant leaving him out of the shared meal (the common supper, which may have fed the idle; compare 3:10), social distance in daily life, or a formal step in church discipline. The churches' practices of discipline, and how 3:14-15 limits it, are compared on the card on the chapter page.
orig: στέλλεσθαι ὑμᾶς (stellesthai hymas)

p: Paul supported himself by his craft, giving up his right to support so that the church would have a pattern to imitate.
b: Acts says Paul and Aquila worked at the same trade in Corinth: "Their craft was making tents" (Acts 18:3). 1 Thessalonians 2:9 uses nearly the same words as this verse. Paul says he had the "right" (exousia) to be supported, as he argues at length in 1 Corinthians 9, recalling Jesus' saying that "a worker has earned his pay" (Luke 10:7). He gave it up, he says here, "to make ourselves a pattern for you, so that you would imitate us" (3:9). The verb is mimeomai, "imitate": 1 Thessalonians 1:6 says the readers had already become imitators of the apostles and of the Lord (compare 1 Corinthians 11:1). Paul's "tradition" about work (3:6) included the way he lived among them.
r: Acts 18:3; Acts 20:34; 1 Thessalonians 2:9; 1 Corinthians 4:12; 2 Corinthians 11:9; 1 Corinthians 11:1; 1 Corinthians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 1:6; Philippians 3:17; 3:9; 1 Corinthians 9:4-18; Luke 10:7; Matthew 10:10; 2 Corinthians 11:7-9

a: Whoever does not want to work should not eat either
t: 'Not willing to work': who, and why?
p: The rule is for those who will not work, not those who cannot. Why some stopped working is debated.
b: The Greek is "if anyone is not willing to work": it concerns refusal, not inability. The sick, the old and the widows are not in view (compare 1 Timothy 5:3-16). It echoes the curse on Adam, "By the sweat of your face you will eat bread" (Genesis 3:19), and Jewish wisdom on idleness (Proverbs 6:6-11; Proverbs 10:4). Why did some stop working? (1) End-time excitement: thinking the day had come (2:2), they left their work; this is the traditional explanation. (2) A social cause: R. Russell argued (1988) that a social explanation fits the evidence better, pointing to the dependence of the poor on benefactors in Greek and Roman cities: poorer members may have lived on richer believers, and the church's shared meals made it easy. The saying had a long later life: Lenin called it "the socialist principle" (The State and Revolution, 1917), and the 1936 Soviet constitution wrote it into article 12.
l: He who does not work, neither shall he eat
He who does not work, neither shall he eat

t: Mark out, and do not mix
p: Take note of him publicly, and do not keep company with him.
b: Semeiousthe, "mark, take note of", from semeion, "sign": the church is to note who refuses the letter's word. Synanamignysthai, "mix with", is the verb of 1 Corinthians 5: "do not mix with anyone who is called a brother and who is a sexual sinner" (1 Corinthians 5:11). There the offender is removed from the church (1 Corinthians 5:13); here, by contrast, he is still a brother (3:15). The goal is shame (entrapei), a turning back, not punishment. "Through the letter" may go with "our word" (the word given in this letter, as the Plain English Translation takes it) or with "mark" (note him, and tell us by letter).
orig: σημειοῦσθε, μὴ συναναμίγνυσθαι (semeiousthe, me synanamignysthai)

p: Not an enemy, but a brother to be warned: the limit that churches with very different discipline cite.
b: Noutheteite, "warn, correct, admonish", is what a family member does. The verse sets a limit on 3:14: shame, not shunning as an enemy. Jesus' rule in Matthew 18 also begins with a brother: "If your brother sins against you, go and correct him" (Matthew 18:15), though there a final step treats him "as you regard the Gentile and the tax collector" (Matthew 18:17). The Mennonite Dordrecht Confession (1632) cites both sides of this passage: 3:14 for shunning the separated, and 3:15 for its limit, "we must not count them as enemies, but admonish them as brethren" (article 17). See the card.
orig: νουθετεῖτε ὡς ἀδελφόν (noutheteite hos adelphon)

p: Paul's usual closing is 'the God of peace'; here it is the Lord Jesus.
b: Paul often blesses with "the God of peace": "The God of peace be with all of you. Amen" (Romans 15:33; compare Romans 16:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:23). Only here is it "the Lord of peace", and in this letter "the Lord" is usually Jesus (1:7-8; 2:8). The wish for peace answers the turmoil of the letter: persecution (1:4), alarm about the day (2:2), disorder in the church (3:6-12). The closing grace (3:18) is that of 1 Thessalonians 5:28 with one added word, "all": after a chapter about members who live out of line, the blessing does not leave them out.
orig: ὁ κύριος τῆς εἰρήνης (ho kyrios tes eirenes)
r: Romans 15:33; Romans 16:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:23; Numbers 6:26; John 14:27; 3:18; 1 Thessalonians 5:28

a: The greeting is in my own hand, Paul's
p: Paul dictated his letters and wrote the last lines himself, as a sign that they were his.
b: Letters were usually written by a scribe; the sender might add a greeting in his own hand. Romans names its scribe, Tertius (Romans 16:22). Paul's own closing appears in 1 Corinthians 16:21, in the same words: "The greeting is in my own hand, Paul's" (1 Corinthians 16:21), and in Galatians 6:11, Colossians 4:18 and Philemon 19. Here he adds that it is "the sign in every letter", which answers the worry about a letter "that seems to be from us" (2:2). Scholars who think a follower wrote the letter take the stress on the signature as the clearest mark of imitation; those who think Paul wrote it take it as his natural reply to a forgery. On the view that Paul wrote it, the first readers would have seen a change of handwriting at this point in the original.
